COPART $CPRT PAID $1.9 BILLION TO STOP DEPENDING ON CAR CRASHES - SIX LEN5ES, SIX NAMES:

Six Len5es, six names, and what they share is not an industry. Every one is paid by repetition - a filter that clogs, a toolbox bought on installments, a shift that needs covering, a loan that rolls over, a ham. The verdict on the name at the top: a record share of damaged cars is now written off, Copart handled fewer of them anyway, and Thursday night's $1.9 billion is the company conceding that its own repetition is slowing.

Copart at $31.82 (after hours), +$1.87 / +6.24% from Friday's $29.95 close, after a regular close of $31.72, +$1.77 / +5.91%. The Dallas company runs the online auctions where insurers sell cars they have decided are not worth repairing.

Reported after the close on Thursday, September 10, for the three months to July 31: revenue $1.15B, +2.4%; profit $0.35 a share, -14.6%, against the $0.38 carried; cars sold worldwide -2.9%, US insurance volumes -7.5%, average price +3.5%. Dearer cars covering for fewer cars. Total loss frequency - the share of damaged cars an insurer junks instead of repairing - hit a record 23.3% for a June quarter against 22.4%, and still did not help, because collision claims fell 3.4% in a year.

So that same night Copart agreed to buy ACV Auctions at $10.41, unchanged today, for $10.50 a share in cash. ACV sells no wrecks. It runs the dealer-to-dealer market in trade-ins and off-lease cars with clean titles, over 800,000 a year, and in chief executive Jay Adair's words "operates with virtually no land of its own." Copart sold more than 4 million cars out of hundreds of physical yards. It is buying its own opposite. ACV fits none of the six styles weighed here, its price now simply the offer.

WATCH the domestic insurance car count, not revenue. WHEN: the tender offer - the formal invitation to ACV holders to sell - must open within seven business days of Thursday's agreement, with closing expected by end-December; first-quarter results are tentatively November 19. RISK: ACV trades nine cents under the offer, and a $115.3M reverse termination fee is what Copart owes if regulators block it.

MOMENTUM LEN5:
ManpowerGroup at $59.15 (after hours), +$2.69 / +4.76% from Friday's $56.46 close; the regular day ended $58.03. The Milwaukee firm finds people work and bills the employer. Fifth of thirty; this Len5 wants the recent and longer climbs to agree near a one-year high, and only the longer does: +135% off February's $25.15 low but 7.4% under August 28's $63.88. July 16: revenue $4.9B, +8%; $0.99 a share with one-off items set aside, against a $1.44 loss a year ago. CHANGE IT: a close above $63.88, or a third quarter under the $1.01 carried for October 15. VERDICT: a bet on other firms hiring, already priced for the recovery it describes.

QUALITY-VALUE LEN5:
Copart again, third of fifty-four, weighed rather than repeated. This Len5 wants a business nobody could rebuild, bought under its worth. The rebuild half is not arguable: licensed yards outside every American city, plus the insurer contracts to fill them, is not something a rival assembles. The price half is 19.3 times profit, 35.0% under last September's $48.96. Third rather than first is the cheque just written, which tops the $1.48B earned all fiscal year and leaves just over $2B of the $4.5B held, still with no borrowings. CHANGE IT: domestic insurance cars rising again with no purchase inside the number.

DEEP-VALUE & SPECIAL-SITUATIONS LEN5:
Donaldson at $87.93 (after hours), -$1.32 / -1.48% today. The Minneapolis firm makes the filters that keep dirt out of engines and factory air. Fifth of fifty-one; this Len5 wants settled earning power cheaply, and a filter is settled by design: sell the housing, then the replacements for the machine's life. August 26: sales $1,058.8M, +8.0%, of which replacement filters were $511.6M, +9.4% - about half the company and its fastest-growing part. CHANGE IT: the aftermarket slipping while new equipment carries the $4.22-$4.38 mapped for fiscal 2027; tentatively December 3. VERDICT: 23.2 times profit is full price for a filter maker, hence fifth.

GROWTH LEN5:
U.S. Bancorp at $62.82 (after hours), -$0.02 / -0.03% today. The Minneapolis bank takes deposits, lends, and processes card payments for shops. First of thirty on a Len5 wanting growth the price has not charged for, and 12.5 times profit is the lowest price here. July 16: net income $2,177M, +20%; $1.35 a share, +22%, against $1.27 carried - a seventh straight quarter above it - with fee income +13.2% growing faster than lending's +7.5%. CHANGE IT: the Federal Reserve decides Wednesday, September 16 at 2:00pm ET from a range of 3.50%-3.75% unmoved all year, and a bank's net interest margin - what it keeps on loans after paying depositors, 2.79% here - moves first. VERDICT: that growth at that price, paying 3.4% a year, ex-dividend September 30.

HYPERGROWTH LEN5:
Wise at $12.13 (after hours), +$0.11 / +0.92% today. The Jersey company runs the app for sending money abroad without a bank's exchange-rate markup. Sixth of thirty on a Len5 wanting a business early as well as fast. Fast is settled - July 16: net revenue $714.0M, +25%, on $69.3B moved across borders, +26%. Early is the odd half, because Wise is becoming something else: transaction fees were $540.9M of that revenue, customers now leave $41.2B parked in their accounts earning $225.4M of interest, and activity other than sending money abroad is 51% of the total. CHANGE IT: central banks write that interest line, not Wise, so transfers must grow fast enough to carry a rate-cutting cycle; Wise set October 15. VERDICT: 24.6 times profit, and over half the business is no longer the thing Wise is for.

INCOME LEN5:
Smithfield Foods at $20.31 (after hours), +$0.05 / +0.25% today, after a one-year low of $20.05 on Friday. The Virginia company raises hogs and makes packaged pork. Fourth of thirty on a Len5 wanting cash reaching owners that the business itself funds: $0.3125 a quarter, $1.25 a year, about 6.2% here, much the largest yield on this board, with borrowings net of cash at only 0.4 times a year's cash profit. The cash is the objection. August 11, first half: a record $638M of adjusted operating profit, yet running the business produced $204M, $165M went into plant and equipment, and the $39M left sits against roughly $246M of dividends. CHANGE IT: the second half is when hams sell, so a full year where spare cash covers the payment; tentatively October 27. VERDICT: the yield is real and the first half did not earn it in cash.

Americans crash less often now, and wreck cars more expensively when they do. Copart has spent 44 years perfecting the second half of that sentence and has no answer to the first. On Thursday it paid $1.9 billion for one, and competition regulators decide whether it gets to keep it.

text:
Faster Growth Still Leaves a Debt Problem

Scott Bessent’s 3% growth argument offers Washington an attractive possibility: expand the economy fast enough to make a heavy debt burden easier to carry.

The difficulty for bondholders is that a larger economy can improve the outlook while leaving the government’s borrowing requirement high enough for debt to keep rising relative to output.

Improvement is not stabilization

The Wall Street Journal analysis describes a CBO-based productivity scenario that raises growth to 2.4% and puts debt at 109% of GDP after a decade, versus a 120% baseline.

The ratio is lower than the baseline, but it continues climbing under that scenario, so the result illustrates relief rather than a completed fiscal repair.

These are conditional projections, not measured outcomes or a promise that AI adoption will generate the assumed productivity gain.

Bessent’s preferred growth rate also needs to be sustained, which makes a strong quarter or a burst of investment inadequate evidence that the fiscal path has changed.

The interest-cost catch

Higher productivity can lift tax receipts, but it can also increase investment demand and interest rates, raising the cost of servicing outstanding debt.

The WSJ analysis says higher debt-service costs consume more than one-third of the additional revenue in the CBO-based scenario.

That interaction matters because the government already carries a large debt stock, making the price of borrowing an important offset to the benefits of faster output.

An aging population adds another constraint, limiting labor-force expansion and leaving productivity to do more of the work needed to sustain faster growth.

The bond-market test

My read is that an AI productivity boom strengthens the fiscal outlook without automatically removing Treasury supply or refinancing pressure from the investment case.

Evidence of improvement would include durable productivity gains, stronger revenues relative to spending and a structural budget gap that actually narrows.

If growth accelerates while the borrowing requirement remains large, investors could still demand compensation for financing costs and the uncertainty around future fiscal adjustment.

Bottom line

Growth can make the debt burden more manageable, but a scenario with a smaller, still-rising debt ratio does not justify treating fiscal risk as solved.

COINBASE $COIN GAINED $4.3 BILLION TODAY ON A VOTE THAT HAPPENS TOMORROW AT 2:15PM:

Coinbase at $188.10 (after hours), +$12.84 / +7.33% from Friday's $175.26 close, after finishing the regular day at $191.44, +$16.18 / +9.23%. The New York company, 4,951 employees, founded 2012, runs the biggest cryptocurrency exchange in the United States and takes a fee on every trade.

The verdict: nothing happened to this business today. A bill got a new draft, an analyst who had the stock at Sell moved to Neutral, and the market paid about $4.3 billion for the pair - $46.2B of company on Friday, $50.5B tonight.

Sunday night, Senate Republicans released a revised draft of the CLARITY Act, the bill that would settle which American regulator supervises digital coins: the Securities and Exchange Commission for anything counted as a security, the Commodity Futures Trading Commission for everything else. The new text takes in 126 changes Democrats asked for. Tomorrow, Tuesday September 15 at 2:15pm ET, the Senate votes on whether to begin formally debating it at all - 60 votes needed, against 53 Republican seats, so at least seven Democrats or independents have to cross. Two did in May, when the Senate Banking Committee moved it along 15-9. And the vote does not pass the bill. It decides whether the Senate may argue about it.

Separately, Compass Point analyst Ed Engel raised Coinbase from Sell to Neutral, target price $177 from $130. Read that twice: the upgrade is to Neutral, and the target sits $11.10 below where the shares trade tonight.

One figure frames the day. Polymarket, where people bet real money on outcomes, prices the CLARITY Act becoming law this year near 30% - up hard from about 12% earlier this month, so the draft moved something real, and still a market saying the thing most likely does not happen.

The business went the other way. July 30, after the close, for the three months to June 30:

- Net revenue $1.22B against $1.50B a year earlier - about 18% less money coming in
- Trading fees $599M, down 21% from the previous three months
- Subscriptions and services $555M, the largest share of the total that half has ever carried, still 12% below a year ago
- A net loss of $359.5M, where analysts had carried $0.14 a share of profit
- Cash profit before interest, tax and wear on equipment: $207.8M, a fourteenth straight positive quarter

Three quarters running have now filed a loss: $666.7M, then $394.1M, then $359.5M. That is $1.42B, and it leaves no profit in the last twelve months.

One line points the other way, and it is the real case for owning this. Coinbase handled a record 10.3% of the world's crypto trading last quarter, up from 9.1% three months before, on $146.4B of trades. It is winning a bigger share of a shrinking pot.

Now the part nobody cheering today has priced. The same draft hands the Treasury secretary power to temporarily restrict stablecoin rewards if they start pulling deposits out of small community banks. Stablecoins are digital dollars, each meant to be backed one-for-one by a real dollar; Coinbase pays people to hold them and earns interest on the pile, and that income sits inside the subscriptions line - close to half of all revenue. Average USDC held on its platform hit $20B last quarter, more than 30% of every one in existence. The bill Coinbase spent today celebrating carries a switch pointed at its own engine.

Two prices say today was about Washington, not crypto. Bitcoin sits at $78,390, +$830 / +1.07% since midnight. Robinhood Markets at $113.93 (after hours), +$1.36 / +1.21% from Friday's $112.57 close, is the other place Americans buy coins in an app; it closed the regular day +1.55%. Coinbase closed +9.23%. Same session, same asset, three different answers. Robinhood is on none of the six Len5es either, and price is why: at about 50 times the last year of profit and 10.7 times book value - what owners would keep after selling everything and paying every debt - neither value Len5 is offered a discount.

This was not just a morning pop. The stock opened at $180.98, already $5.72 / +3.26% up before a share traded in the session, then added another $10.46 across the day on 13.2M shares against a two-week average of 8.1M.

VERDICT: a much higher price for a company that has lost money three quarters running, bought on a probability rather than a result. Coinbase is not a pick on any of the six Len5es, and the reason is arithmetic rather than opinion - both value Len5es need profit to divide a price by and there is none, the Len5 hunting businesses that are early as well as fast gets a $50.5B company with revenue going backwards, and there is no dividend for the Income Len5 to count. Momentum is the near miss: $188.10 sits 35.2% above the $139.11 low of July 31, the recent half of that test, while the $402.16 set on October 10 last year flatly disagrees, leaving the stock 53.2% under it. A filed profit changes the value reads; a run back toward that high changes the momentum one.

WATCH the share of revenue that is not trading fees, not the coin price - that half is near fifty cents on the dollar, and the stablecoin income inside it is what the new bill can reach. RISK: at 3.5 times book value with no earnings underneath, a failed vote takes back the only thing that was bought today.

A trading day is meant to tell you what a business is worth. Today it told you what a hundred senators might do at a quarter past two tomorrow afternoon, and charged $4.3 billion for the guess. In the same quarter, Coinbase sold less, lost money, and won more of the market than it ever has. None of those three is what moved.

🗞️ Wilkes-Barre Times Leader · September 14, 1926 · Page 1

Wilkes-Barre police are searching today for a young man accused of attempting to sexually assault a 17 year old Plymouth girl before throwing her from his automobile early this morning.

Anna Felnock, 17, of 712 Temperance Hill, Plymouth, left home around 6:30 a.m. for her job at the Palace Laundry on North Washington Street. While waiting for a bus at Carey Avenue and Division Street, a young man driving a Ford coupe offered her a ride into town.

Felnock accepted. Instead of taking her directly to the Square, however, the driver traveled along Carey Avenue and Academy Street to South Franklin Street. Between South and Northampton streets, he stopped the car and allegedly attempted to assault her.

Felnock fought him off. The man then threw her from the automobile and sped away.

Charles Zimmer of 60 Davis Place and another man came upon Felnock lying in the street several minutes later. They carried her into the nearby home of Mrs. Frances Weaver, 105 South Franklin Street, and police were summoned.

Felnock was taken to Wilkes-Barre General Hospital suffering from bruises and contusions of the right knee and elbow, along with shock.

Captain Eckert of the traffic squad and Philip Eckert are searching for the driver. Felnock told police the man claimed to work somewhere on the “mountain,” and authorities believe that information may lead to his arrest.

Police called the case one of the worst of its kind reported to them in some time.

Name one country on earth that would not want Canada’s geographic position: a shared continent, an integrated industrial base, and an imaginary line between us and the largest, richest market in the world. That is not a slogan. That is the country we actually live in.Carney can sell the European line to a room that already wants to hear it. His supporters will nod because it lets them feel worldly without looking at a map. They treat Canada like a finishing school for European manners: same flag, different continent, different neighbours, different problems. They lecture about values while the country that trades, works, freezes, and pays the bills on this side of the Atlantic is treated as an embarrassment to be managed.

Then they act shocked by the arithmetic.

About 72 percent of Canada’s goods exports still go to the United States. In some recent months that share has fallen into the mid-60s, not because Ottawa discovered a new continent, but because the relationship is being broken on purpose. Roughly three-fifths of our merchandise imports still come from the U.S. The honest point is simpler: we need that market far more than it needs ours. A trade war with your largest customer is not courage. It is a bet that slogans can replace customers.

Walking away from talks at the eleventh hour does not change that. Here is what happened. After weeks of negotiations, the talks collapsed late on the deadline. Washington said it had offered Canada the most preferential treatment of any major exporter. Ottawa said the last-minute terms were a bad deal, suspended negotiations, and sent its team home. Fine. Argue the terms. Do not pretend Canada can casually replace three-quarters of its export market with Europe and a press release.

And do not rewrite the scoreboard of that night. Foolish Liberals cheered as if Carney had just bodychecked the big bad orange man. Elbows up. Never 51. A hockey slogan instead of a customer.

More than eleven years ago, the United States was not treated as an enemy. It was treated as a partner. That is the relationship this country was built on. Now the same crowd that cannot look at a map wants to pick a fight with the market that keeps the lights on.

And do not even get me started on the outrageous immigration taking place while all of this is happening.

Some of us look at the pattern and draw a harder conclusion. Carney is in cahoots with Trump to cripple Canada until the only option left is for the United States to annex us. For me, it cannot happen soon enough. I am 100 percent Canadian. That makes me 100 percent North American.

Do not rewrite the economic scoreboard either. Canada was the only G7 country, and for a stretch the only G20 country, to slip into a technical recession: two straight quarters of shrinking GDP in late 2025 and early 2026. Growth has since ticked back up. That does not erase the damage: weak per-capita growth, businesses getting hit, companies uprooting to the States, and households falling further behind.

Meanwhile Ottawa boasts of more than $26 billion in aid to Ukraine since 2022. Food Banks Canada recorded nearly 2.2 million visits in a single month — the highest number they have ever counted. Visits have more than doubled since 2019. One in four people in this country now lives with food insecurity. You can support Ukraine and still notice that Canadians are lining up for groceries. A government that cannot hold both thoughts at once is not serious.

If the Canada they want is a European talking point with a maple-leaf sticker, they should say so. Stop wrapping a transatlantic rebrand in patriotism while the North American advantage — the one thing almost every other country would kill for — is being talked away.

The contract is where the deal is either protected or exposed.

10 C.A.R. forms California agents should understand:

RPA-CA — Residential Purchase Agreement
    The offer: price, deposit, loan terms, contingencies, escrow timing, possession, costs, included/excluded items.
RLA — Residential Listing Agreement
    Seller relationship: term, list price, compensation, MLS instructions, exclusions, marketing, broker authority.
BRBC — Buyer Representation and Broker Compensation Agreement
    Buyer relationship, term, compensation, broker duties, buyer duties, and exclusivity if selected.
SPQ — Seller Property Questionnaire
    Seller disclosures: repairs, defects, permits, water issues, insurance claims, legal issues, material facts.
TDS — Transfer Disclosure Statement
    Seller property condition disclosure and agent visual inspection section.
AVID — Agent Visual Inspection Disclosure
    What the agent visually observes. Not a contractor report. Not a home inspection.
CR — Contingency Removal
    Used when buyers remove loan, appraisal, investigation, sale of property, or other contingencies.
RR — Request for Repair
    Buyer requests repairs, credits, price changes, or corrections after investigation.
RRRR — Seller Response and Buyer Reply to Request for Repair
    Controls the repair negotiation.
COP — Contingency for Sale of Buyer’s Property
    Used when the buyer needs to sell another property to close.

Forms are not paperwork.

They control terms, timing, disclosure, leverage, risk, compensation, and expectations.

Know what you are putting in front of people.

Merck & Co. at $145.48 (after hours), +$1.55 / +1.08% today, and Moderna at $146.40 (after hours), +$2.43 / +1.69% today, said their INTerpath-001 trial worked: a cancer vaccine built individually for each patient, given with Keytruda, held melanoma off after surgery longer than Keytruda alone - the first of its kind to clear a late-stage trial. The sequencing that picks that vaccine's targets out of each patient's tumor is Personalis's work.

Tempus rose 24.1% that day and hit $72.69 by August 21. The best week of news in Personalis's history lifted its buyer by nearly half and lifted what Personalis owners collect by nothing. On July 17 that $16.25 meant 0.3097 Tempus shares; tonight it means 0.2621. And the stock has closed above $16.25 in sixteen of the seventeen sessions since August 20, as high as $18.38. A deal at a set value normally trades a shade under it; this one trades over. That is people paying for a raise nobody has offered.

Momentum is the Len5 watching it, second of thirty. That style wants a price near the top of its one-year range with the recent climb and the longer one agreeing, and both hold: $4.955 on April 29 up to $18.89 on August 21, today 13.8% under that. The engine is no longer its own. August 4 brought June-quarter revenue of $22.4M, +30%, the clinical test itself only $2.6M of it, and a loss widening to $0.30 a share from $0.23 - none of which moves this price now. CHANGE IT: Tempus's fifteen-day average slipping under $48.42, which turns a fixed value into a fixed share count and sends these owners downhill on somebody else's ride.

VERDICT: a real breakout whose remaining upside belongs to the buyer. WATCH the $16.25, not the test volumes; forecasts and quarterly calls stopped when the papers were signed. WHEN: no meeting date is set - the voting documents went in at the start of September, with a backstop deadline of April 20, 2027. RISK: about $76.8M is owed either way if this breaks. None of the other three is on a Len5: Tempus and Moderna are loss-makers, leaving the value styles no profit to divide a price by, and Merck at 115 times profit is the opposite complaint.

QUALITY-VALUE LEN5:
Arch Capital Group at $97.42 (after hours), +$1.33 / +1.38% today, runner-up of fifty-four, insures specialist risks and reinsures other insurers out of Bermuda. This Len5 wants a business nobody could rebuild bought under its worth, and the unbuyable part is refusing business at a bad price: on July 28 claims and costs took 83.5 cents of every premium dollar despite $201M of catastrophe losses, at 7.5 times profit. WATCH the tentative October 26 report, where $1.85 is carried against the $2.56 just earned - that gap is hurricane season, and it is the risk. VERDICT: the deepest discount here, priced for a bad autumn that has not come.

DEEP-VALUE & SPECIAL-SITUATIONS LEN5:
Broadridge Financial Solutions at $174.39 (after hours), +$6.65 / +3.96% today, runner-up of fifty-one, sends the ballot when a company you own through a broker calls a vote. This Len5 wants settled earning power bought cheaply, and settled means fees billed again every year: $4.9B of recurring revenue, +8% in the year to June 30, record signings of $305M, at about 18 times the $9.60 it earned with one-off items set aside, 31.8% under last September's high. WATCH next Monday, September 21, when comments close on a Securities and Exchange Commission proposal to make electronic delivery the default instead of paper - postage is the risk. VERDICT: a record year at a third off.

GROWTH LEN5:
ServisFirst Bancshares at $42.30 (after hours), +$0.17 / +0.40% today, runner-up of thirty, lends to businesses and well-off households across the South with almost no branches - 666 people running a $4.6B company. This Len5 wants profit growth the price has not already charged for, and none of this was bought: July 20 brought net income of $85.8M against $61.4M, +39.7%, loans up $532.6M in three months, and a net interest margin - what a bank keeps on loans after paying depositors - of 3.63%, wider by 0.53 points in a year, at 14.4 times profit. WATCH whether that loan pace holds once the margin stops widening, tentatively October 19. RISK: lending aimed at the fastest-growing states turns first when those states cool. VERDICT: 40% growth at an ordinary price.

HYPERGROWTH LEN5:
AppLovin at $333.05 (after hours), +$9.09 / +2.81% today, runner-up of thirty, runs the system that decides which advert appears inside a mobile app, and does it with 898 people. This Len5 wants a business early as well as fast. Fast is settled: August 5 brought revenue of $1.92B, +53%, and cash profit before interest, tax and wear on equipment of $1.61B - 84 cents of every revenue dollar. Early is the half holding it back, since a $111.8B company is what rivals try to displace. The figure to sit with is the beat itself: $3.76 a share against $3.75 carried, one cent, after 20, 7, 31 and 12 cents in the four quarters before it. VERDICT: growing 53% and clearing its own bar by less each time, $4.01 carried for November 4.

INCOME LEN5:
Euroseas at $74.80 (after hours), +$0.24 / +0.32% today, runner-up of thirty, owns 21 containerships and rents them out on charters measured in years. This Len5 wants cash reaching owners that the business itself funds, and the cover is close to absurd: the August 13 quarter earned $4.70 a share against $4.29 carried, while the dividend is $0.80 - about 17 cents of every dollar earned. That is $3.20 a year, near 4.3% here, paid on Wednesday. What holds it a step back is the building program: twelve more ships by 2029, taking the fleet from 21 to 33, out of that same cash. RISK: only 2.6M of its 6.6M shares trade freely, so a handful of orders sets the price.

Five of these six are arguments about a business. Personalis is not one any more: its worth was settled in a document on July 20, and the only say its owners have left is a vote with no date on it. The post uses a single family photo at a roller rink as visual proof that skipping all childhood vaccines produces healthy kids and that listed ingredients are unnecessary. Anecdotes like this circulate widely in certain circles because healthy unvaccinated children exist, yet they cannot establish population-level safety or necessity; families who remain unvaccinated often differ in diet, healthcare-seeking, and exposure patterns from the general population.

Aluminum salts appear as adjuvants in several routine vaccines (DTaP, hepatitis B, HPV, pneumococcal) at microgram-to-low-milligram levels per dose—amounts well below typical daily dietary intake from food and water. Thimerosal (ethylmercury) was largely removed from U.S. and European childhood schedules two decades ago and remains only in some multi-dose flu vials; it is chemically distinct from the methylmercury found in fish. Formaldehyde is used to inactivate viruses or toxins and leaves residual traces smaller than those naturally present in a pear or apple. Polysorbate 80 functions as an emulsifier and is a common food additive found in ice cream at far higher concentrations. Fetal-cell-line claims refer to the WI-38 and MRC-5 cell lines derived from two elective abortions in the 1960s; these immortalized cell cultures are used to grow certain viruses during manufacturing (rubella, varicella, and others), but the finished vaccine contains neither fetal cells nor tissue.

The author’s bio and repeated posts rest on virus denialism drawn from Stefan Lanka and Thomas Cowan. Lanka’s 2011 prize offer for measles-virus proof produced a German civil case that turned on the wording of the contest (one paper versus six papers), not on scientific existence; appellate judges explicitly stated that the ruling said nothing about whether the virus exists and noted the scientific consensus that it does. Cowan, who surrendered his California medical license, has promoted terrain theory, 5 G as the cause of COVID, and the view that viruses are cellular waste rather than pathogens. Viruses including measles, polio, and SARS-CoV-2 have been isolated in culture, independently sequenced by many labs, visualized by electron microscopy, and shown to meet adapted Koch-style criteria through animal models and controlled challenge studies.

Large-scale data show vaccines have averted an estimated 154 million deaths since 1974, with the largest gains among infants. Unvaccinated children experience higher rates of the targeted diseases (measles, pertussis, etc.). Observational comparisons of vaccinated versus unvaccinated children for chronic conditions (asthma, developmental delay, allergies) yield mixed results; some smaller practice-based studies report higher odds in the vaccinated group, while larger representative surveys, such as Germany’s KiGGS, find little difference once vaccine-preventable illnesses are excluded. Confounding by lifestyle, diagnostic intensity, and socioeconomic factors remains difficult to eliminate in non-randomized data.
